extraction.name: WikiText
extraction.description: A freely available benchmark corpus for language modeling, introduced to evaluate how well language models can exploit longer contexts and handle more realistic vocabularies and larger corpora.
extraction.creator: Stephen Merity; Caiming Xiong; James Bradbury; Richard Socher
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors constructed a new language modeling dataset from Wikipedia by selecting Good and Featured articles, extracting article text via the Wikipedia API, removing list-heavy sections and HTML leakage, replacing formulae/LaTeX with placeholder tokens, and then normalizing and tokenizing the text before building the vocabulary.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw/source data consisted of text extracted from Wikipedia articles, specifically articles meeting Wikipedia's Good or Featured article criteria, with raw text obtained from Wikipedia markup.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The prior PTB dataset is limited because it lowercases all tokens, removes punctuation, restricts vocabulary to 10k words, is unrealistic for real language use, and lacks a long-tail vocabulary needed for rare words such as named entities. Other existing large-scale datasets are also limited by restrictive licensing or randomized sentence ordering, which is unrealistic and hinders learning/evaluation of long-term dependencies.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a language modeling benchmark/platform, particularly for improving handling of rare words and modeling long-term dependencies, and is made available to the research community.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors state that the Wikipedia-based language modeling dataset will be made available to the community, but no update schedule, maintainer details, or deprecation policy are provided.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: PTB: lower-cased words, replaced numbers with N, replaced newlines with <eos>, removed other punctuation, limited vocabulary to the most frequent 10k words and replaced remaining tokens with <unk>. WikiText: selected only Good/Featured Wikipedia articles, extracted raw text via the Wikipedia API, removed list-heavy sections and leaked HTML artifacts, replaced mathematical formulae and LaTeX code with <formula> tokens, normalized and tokenized with the Moses tokenizer augmented to split numbers, discarded words with count below 3, and mapped out-of-vocabulary words to <unk>.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: The tokens in PTB are all lower case, stripped of any punctuation, and limited to a vocabulary of only 10k words. These limitations mean that the PTB is unrealistic for real language use... the lack of a long tail for the vocabulary is problematic... they either have restrictive licensing which prevents widespread use or have randomized sentence ordering... which is unrealistic for most language use and prevents the effective learning and evaluation of longer term dependencies.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: Hence, we constructed a language modeling dataset using text extracted from Wikipedia and will make this available to the community... We hope this new dataset can serve as a platform to improve handling of rare words and the usage of long term dependencies in language modeling.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: we constructed a language modeling dataset using text extracted from Wikipedia and will make this available to the community.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: “As part of the pre-processing performed by Mikolov et al. (2010), words were lower-cased, numbers were replaced with N, newlines were replaced with ⟨eos⟩, and all other punctuation was removed. The vocabulary is the most frequent 10k words with the rest of the tokens being replaced by an ⟨unk⟩ token.”; “We selected articles only fitting the Good or Featured article criteria... Once extracted, specific sections which primarily featured lists were removed by default. Other minor bugs, such as sort keys and Edit buttons that leaked in from the HTML, were also removed. Mathematical formulae and LATEX code, were replaced with ⟨formula⟩ tokens. Normalization and tokenization were performed using the Moses tokenizer... Following Chelba et al. (2013) a vocabulary was constructed by discarding all words with a count below 3. Words outside of the vocabulary were mapped to the ⟨unk⟩ token”
